topic: South Indian Dynasties (Rashtrakutas, Cholas, Kakatiyas, Hoysalas, Yadavas)

items.question: "The Chola system of local self-government was one of the most advanced of its age." Examine the working of the village assemblies under the Cholas.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Cholas (9th–13th centuries)** are celebrated for a **highly developed system of local self-government**, reconstructed chiefly from the **Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I (c.919–921 CE)** — regarded as **one of the world's earliest documented pieces of evidence of elected local governance**.

The village was the basic unit of administration. It was divided into **thirty wards (kudumbus)**, each nominating candidates who met prescribed qualifications of age, property and integrity. Members were then chosen by **lot — the kudavolai (pot-ticket) system — for a one-year term**, an early form of rotation that limited entrenchment. Governance was handled by **specialised committees (variyams)**: the **samvatsaravariyam (annual committee)**, the **tottavariyam (garden committee)**, the **eri-variyam (tank committee)**, along with the **pancha-variyam** and **pon-variyam (gold committee)**. Members were the **variyapparumakal**; a **judicial committee (nyayattar)** and paid staff (**madhyasthas**) kept village records.

The assembly (**sabha**, whose larger body was the **mahasabha/perunguri**) usually met **in the temple, under a tree or near a tank**. It held **proprietary rights over communal land**, controlled private lands, **reclaimed forest and wasteland**, **assessed and collected land revenue**, could **sell defaulters' land**, and possessed powers of **taxation and remission**. Villages were classified as **Ur** (mixed-caste revenue-paying), **Brahmadeya/agrahara** (tax-free Brahmin grants) and **Devadana** (temple grants).

**AP angle:** the Chola–Vengi link under **Kulottunga I**, who united the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (coastal Andhra)** with the Cholas, carried these administrative practices into the Telugu country. In sum, the elective principle, fixed tenure, committee specialisation and financial autonomy make the Chola village a **remarkably self-reliant institution** — though its base remained land-owning and caste-bound rather than universal.
keyPoints: Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I (c.919–921) = among the world's earliest records of elected local self-government.
Village split into 30 wards (kudumbus); members chosen by lot (kudavolai) for one year.
Committees: samvatsaravariyam (annual), tottavariyam (garden), eri-variyam (tank), pon-variyam (gold); nyayattar (judicial).
Sabha held communal land rights, assessed/collected revenue, could tax, remit and sell defaulters' land.
Village types: Ur, Brahmadeya (agrahara), Devadana; met in temple/under tree/near tank.
AP link: Kulottunga I united Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi with the Cholas.
Limitation: participation was land-owning and caste-bound, not universal.

items.question: Assess the contribution of the Kakatiya dynasty to the political and cultural development of the Telugu region.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Kakatiyas (1163–1323 CE)**, ruling from **Warangal**, were the **first major indigenous power to politically unify the Telugu-speaking regions** of present Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, forging an enduring **Telugu cultural identity**.

**Political consolidation:** Beginning as **Western Chalukya feudatories**, they asserted sovereignty under **Prataparudra I (1163)**. **Ganapati Deva (1198–1262)** unified the Telugu territories, shifted the capital from **Hanumakonda to Warangal (Orugallu)** and integrated feudal chiefs (the **nayankara** system). **Rudrama Devi (1262–1296)**, the **first woman ruler** of the Deccan of her stature, defended the realm and impressed the traveller **Marco Polo**. The dynasty ended when **Prataparudra II** fell to the **Tughlaqs in 1323**, after which the Deccan lay open to the Bahmani Sultanate.

**Economic & irrigation legacy:** The Kakatiyas built an extensive network of **tanks** — **Pakhal** and **Ramappa** lakes — that sustained agriculture for centuries; **Ganapati Deva's Abhaya Sasanam** promoted maritime trade at **Motupalli port**.

**Cultural achievement:** They patronised **Telugu and Sanskrit literature** (Tikkana Somayaji; Jayapa Senani's works on dance/music), and produced a distinctive architecture — the **Ramappa (Rudreswara) Temple**, inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021**, the **Thousand Pillar Temple** at Hanumakonda, **Warangal Fort** and the famous **Kakatiya toranas** (adopted as the state emblem).

**Conclusion:** By unifying the Telugu country, developing irrigation, encouraging trade and nurturing Telugu literature and art, the Kakatiyas laid the **foundation of Telugu regional identity** — a legacy inherited by the Musunuri Nayakas, the Reddi kingdoms and, administratively, by Vijayanagara.
keyPoints: Kakatiyas (Warangal) first politically unified the Telugu regions; began as Western Chalukya feudatories, sovereign under Prataparudra I (1163).
Ganapati Deva unified the territory, shifted capital to Warangal, built Pakhal Lake and promoted Motupalli trade via Abhaya Sasanam.
Rudrama Devi, first woman ruler, praised by Marco Polo; nayankara system integrated feudal chiefs.
Prataparudra II fell to the Tughlaqs in 1323, opening the Deccan to the Bahmani Sultanate.
Tank irrigation (Pakhal, Ramappa) sustained agriculture; enduring economic legacy.
Cultural legacy: Ramappa Temple (UNESCO 2021), Thousand Pillar Temple, Warangal Fort, Kakatiya toranas, Telugu literature.
Legacy inherited by Musunuri Nayakas, Reddi kingdoms and Vijayanagara administration.
